lessonTitle: Planning and Final Report: Schedules, Critical Path and Traceability

blocks.text: A final-year team of five builds a test rig. They plan 20 weeks, but in week 9 the machined parts arrive late and the whole team sits idle until week 12. The delay was avoidable: the late-arriving order was on the critical path, and nobody had recognised which activities could slip without consequence and which could not.

blocks.markdown: A design project is finished on time not by working harder but by knowing what depends on what. **Planning** breaks the work into manageable pieces, shows how they depend on each other, and identifies the chain that fixes the end date. **Reporting** then records the design so that every decision can be traced to a requirement and to evidence. This unit covers the planning tools first and the report structure second.

blocks.title: Work breakdown structure (WBS) and Gantt chart
blocks.text: A **work breakdown structure** divides the whole project into deliverables and then into work packages, each small enough to estimate, assign to one owner and check. A **Gantt chart** plots each work package as a bar against time, with *dependencies* drawn as links (most commonly finish-to-start: B cannot begin until A has finished) and *milestones* shown as zero-duration markers for events such as 'design freeze' or 'prototype delivered'.

blocks.markdown: **Building the plan.** Start from the deliverables (rig, drawings, report, presentation). Break each into work packages until each lasts from a few days to two or three weeks. Estimate a duration for each, and for each ask 'what must be finished before this can start?'. That gives the dependencies. Place milestones where a decision or delivery is checked. The Gantt chart is simply this information drawn against a calendar.

**Critical path and float.** Every route through the dependency network from start to end has a total duration. The **critical path** is the longest route; it fixes the minimum project duration, and any delay to an activity on it delays the finish by the same amount. Activities off the critical path have **float** (or slack), the time they can slip without delaying the end. Float is computed from the earliest start (ES), earliest finish (EF = ES + duration), latest finish (LF) and latest start (LS = LF - duration).

blocks.caption: Total float of an activity, in the same time unit as the durations (weeks). Critical activities have float 0.

blocks.title: Critical path of a rig project
blocks.prompt: Activities (duration in weeks): A requirements 3; B concept design 4 (after A); C detailed design 6 (after B); D procure parts 5 (after B); E build 4 (after C and D); F test 3 (after E). Find the project duration, the critical path and the float of D.

steps.text: The longer route is critical: the project takes 20 weeks along A-B-C-E-F.
D starts at week 7 (end of B) and finishes at week 12. E cannot start before week 13 because C ends at 13, so the latest finish of D is 13.

blocks.answer: Project duration 20 weeks, critical path A-B-C-E-F, and D has 1 week of float.

rows: Options considered and the reasons for choice
Calculations and drawings that define the design
What was met, not met, and next steps
blocks.caption: A report structure in which each decision links to a requirement and evidence.

blocks.markdown: **Structuring the report.** The reader should be able to pick any design decision and follow a chain: *requirement* (what was needed), *decision* (what was chosen), *evidence* (the calculation, analysis or test that shows it works). Number the requirements and cite the number wherever a decision or result addresses it. A decision without a requirement is unjustified; a requirement without evidence is unverified.

blocks.title: Effect of a late supplier
blocks.prompt: In the rig project, procurement D slips to 7 weeks (all other durations unchanged). Find the new project duration and whether the critical path changes.

steps.text: New length of the route through D.
This is longer than the route through C (20 weeks), so the path through D becomes critical.
The project is delayed by $21-20=1$ week, because D used its 1 week of float and then 1 further week.

blocks.answer: The project takes 21 weeks; the critical path moves to A-B-D-E-F.

items: Build the WBS from deliverables down to work packages with one owner each.
Link packages with dependencies and mark milestones.
Compute ES, EF, LS, LF and the float; list the critical activities.
Review the critical activities weekly and use the float of others for resource levelling.
In the report, tag each decision with the requirement it meets and the evidence that supports it.

blocks.title: Float belongs to the path, not only to the activity
blocks.text: If two non-critical activities lie in series on the same route, they share the float: using it on the first leaves less for the second. Check float on the whole route after any slip.

blocks.title: State your dependency type
blocks.text: When drawing a Gantt chart or network, say which dependencies are finish-to-start and give a duration and unit for every activity. Show the longest path explicitly, with the sum written out.

points: A WBS divides the project into owned work packages; a Gantt chart shows durations, dependencies and milestones against time.
The critical path is the longest dependency route and fixes the project duration; float is $LS-ES$ and is zero on the critical path.
A good design report links every decision to a numbered requirement and to evidence from calculation, analysis or test.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes a work breakdown structure?

options.text: A hierarchical division of the project deliverables into work packages that can be estimated and assigned to owners
A bar chart that shows when each activity happens against the calendar
A list of risks ranked by likelihood and severity
The longest path through the activity network

questions.correctOptionText: A hierarchical division of the project deliverables into work packages that can be estimated and assigned to owners

distractorRationale.a: Correct: it breaks the deliverables down into manageable packages.
distractorRationale.b: That describes a Gantt chart, which uses a WBS as input.

questions.explanation: The WBS is about what has to be produced, divided until each package has one owner and a reasonable estimate. The schedule and critical path are then built on it.

questions.stem: On a Gantt chart for a gearbox prototype, a marker with zero duration labelled 'Design freeze' appears at the end of detail design. What is this marker?

options.text: A milestone
A work package
A float
A dependency

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a milestone marks an event or decision point without duration.
distractorRationale.b: A work package has duration and an owner.
distractorRationale.c: Float is the slack of an activity.
distractorRationale.d: A dependency is a link between two activities.

questions.explanation: A milestone is a zero-duration marker used to check progress at a key event. It makes it clear when a decision, such as freezing the design, must be complete.

questions.stem: A test engineer cannot begin the stress analysis until the CAD model has been completed and checked. What dependency should be drawn between the two tasks?

options.text: Finish-to-start: the analysis starts after the CAD model finishes
Start-to-start: the analysis starts at the same time as the CAD model
A milestone linking the two tasks
No link, because they have different owners

questions.correctOptionText: Finish-to-start: the analysis starts after the CAD model finishes

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the second task cannot begin until the first is complete.
distractorRationale.b: This would let analysis start without a finished model.
distractorRationale.c: A milestone is an event and not a dependency type.
distractorRationale.d: Different owners do not remove dependencies.

questions.explanation: Dependencies capture the logic of the work, whatever the owner. Here the analysis needs the finished model, which is a finish-to-start relationship.

questions.stem: In a network of activities, which description fits the critical path?

options.text: The longest route from start to finish, whose activities have zero float
The route with the largest number of activities
The shortest route, which can be finished first
The route with the most expensive tasks

questions.correctOptionText: The longest route from start to finish, whose activities have zero float

distractorRationale.a: Correct: it fixes the minimum project duration, with no slack.
distractorRationale.b: Length in time and not count of activities decides it.
distractorRationale.c: The shortest route has the most float and does not fix the duration.
distractorRationale.d: Cost does not determine the critical path.

questions.explanation: The finish date cannot come earlier than the longest chain of dependent activities. Activities on that chain have zero float.

questions.stem: In a project report, which entry best links a design decision to requirement and evidence?

options.text: 'Requirement R4 (shaft deflection under 0.1 mm): 40 mm shaft chosen; hand calculation in Appendix C gives 0.06 mm.'
'The 40 mm shaft was chosen because it felt right after much discussion.'
'The shaft is shown in Figure 7.'
'Calculations were carried out by the team.'

questions.correctOptionText: 'Requirement R4 (shaft deflection under 0.1 mm): 40 mm shaft chosen; hand calculation in Appendix C gives 0.06 mm.'

distractorRationale.a: Correct: it cites a requirement, states a decision and points to evidence.
distractorRationale.b: It gives no requirement or evidence.
distractorRationale.c: A figure alone does not say which requirement it serves or why.
distractorRationale.d: It says calculations exist without showing the result.

questions.explanation: A traceable decision names the requirement it meets, states the choice and cites evidence the reader can check. The other statements leave the reader unable to verify anything.

questions.stem: A small project has activity A (2 weeks), then B (5 weeks) and C (3 weeks) both starting after A, then D (4 weeks) starting after both B and C, then E (2 weeks) after D. Find the minimum project duration in weeks.
questions.explanation: The route through B has $2+5+4+2=13$ weeks and the route through C has $2+3+4+2=11$ weeks. The longer route, 13 weeks, fixes the duration.

questions.stem: For the same project (A 2 weeks; B 5 weeks and C 3 weeks after A; D 4 weeks after B and C; E 2 weeks after D), find the total float of activity C, in weeks.
questions.explanation: C starts at week 2 and ends at week 5, but D cannot start until B finishes at week 7. The float is $7-5=2$ weeks.

questions.stem: In another plan, X (4 weeks) comes first; Y (6 weeks) and Z (3 weeks) both follow X; W (5 weeks) follows both Y and Z. Activity Z slips and takes 8 weeks instead of 3. By how many weeks is the project finish delayed?
questions.explanation: The original duration is $4+6+5=15$ weeks and Z has 3 weeks of float. With Z at 8 weeks the route X-Z-W is $4+8+5=17$ weeks, so the project is delayed $17-15=2$ weeks.

questions.stem: You are planning a student team project to design and build a small hydraulic press. List a work breakdown of at least eight work packages in two levels, give three dependencies between them with their type, and identify two milestones.
markingGuide: Top-level deliverables (for example press frame, hydraulic circuit, controls, documentation)
At least eight sensible work packages beneath these, each with one owner
Dependencies stated as finish-to-start with correct logic (design before manufacture, manufacture before assembly)
At least two milestones with zero duration (for example design freeze, first pressure test)
questions.explanation: A good plan decomposes deliverables to estimable packages, links them logically and places milestones at decision points. Wrong logic, such as building before the design is frozen, would be penalised.

questions.stem: A draft report says: 'We chose a plastic gear to reduce noise. The gear is shown in Figure 5. It passed testing.' Rewrite or critique it so that the decision is traceable to a requirement and to evidence, and explain what structure you would give the report so that a reader can trace every decision.
markingGuide: Identifies missing requirement (for example numbered noise limit in dB)
Identifies missing evidence (test method, result with value and unit)
Rewritten with requirement ID, decision, rationale, and reference to calculation or test record
Report structure: requirements, concept selection, detailed design, verification, conclusions with cross references
Traceability matrix or numbering to link requirements to evidence
Notes that a requirement with no evidence is unverified, and a decision with no requirement is unjustified
questions.explanation: A traceable report lets the reader follow requirement, decision and evidence. The draft gives a vague outcome without a number, so a reader cannot check it against anything.
